title: I Set Sail for Distant Lands
content_zh:
My father had a small estate in Nottinghamshire; I was the third of five sons. At fourteen, he sent me to Emanuel College in Cambridge, where I resided three years, applying myself closely to my studies.
I always fancied myself a traveler. The sea called to me with a voice I could not resist. I studied navigation, mathematics, and medicine with equal intensity, preparing for a life of discovery.
My first voyage was aboard the Swallow, under Captain Abraham Pannell. We sailed to the Levant. The journey was uneventful, but I learned the rhythms of the sea — the creak of the hull, the snap of the sails, the thousand small rituals that kept men alive between the sky and the abyss.
On May 4, 1699, I sailed from Bristol aboard the Antelope, bound for the South Seas. The voyage began with fair winds and high hopes. We charted a course through waters where no European had sailed before.
Twelve days out, a violent storm struck from the northwest. The Antelope was driven helpless before the gale, her masts splintering like toothpicks. For a full day and night, we fought to keep the ship afloat.
On the morning of the second day, the lookout cried 'Breakers ahead!' Through the pouring rain, I saw the jagged rocks. The ship struck. The hull splintered. I was thrown into the sea.
I swam for what felt like hours, the waves battering me without mercy. My strength was failing, my limbs numb. I could feel the cold embrace of the deep pulling me down when my feet suddenly touched sand.
I crawled onto a beach and collapsed. The world went dark. When I awakened, I could not move. Thousands of tiny cords bound me to the earth — each one no thicker than a thread of silk. I was pinned like Gulliver to the ground. And that, of course, was my name.
